subject: physics
title: Changes of state
key_idea: Melting, freezing, boiling, evaporating, condensing and sublimating are changes of state. They are physical changes. The particles stay the same, so the mass is conserved and the material recovers its original properties if the change is reversed.

blocks.text: A change of state turns a solid, liquid or gas into another state. This section names the six changes and shows what happens to the particles as a substance is heated.

rows: Gas, directly, without becoming a liquid

items: Heating can cause melting, boiling, evaporating and sublimating.
Cooling can cause freezing and condensing.
Sublimation can also run in reverse, from a gas directly to a solid.

diagram.alt: Change the temperature of water and watch its particles change state.

items: Melting: solid to liquid. Freezing: liquid to solid.
Boiling and evaporating: liquid to gas. Condensing: gas to liquid.
Sublimating: solid directly to gas.

blocks.text: The arrangement and movement of the particles change with the state. The particles themselves do not change.
Heating a solid to a liquid

items: In a solid, the particles are in a regular pattern, vibrating about fixed positions.
In a liquid, the particles are in a random arrangement and move freely.
While the solid melts, the temperature stays constant. The energy goes into the potential energy of the particles.
Once it has melted, more heating makes the particles move faster, so the temperature rises again.

blocks.text: Cooling a gas to a solid

items: As a gas cools, the particles slow down.
Gas to liquid: the particles change from being spread apart to touching each other.
Liquid to solid: the particles change from a random arrangement to a regular pattern, and from moving freely to vibrating in fixed positions.
Attractive forces between the particles are stronger in a solid than in a liquid. In a gas the forces are negligible.
During a change of state the temperature stays constant.
Solid: regular pattern, vibrating in fixed positions. Liquid: random arrangement, moving freely.
Cooling slows the particles down. The energy changes are in the internal energy note.

sections.heading: Physical changes and conservation of mass

blocks.text: Changes of state are physical changes. This section covers why the mass stays the same and how a physical change differs from a chemical change.

items: The particles are rearranged, but none are gained or lost. The number of particles stays the same.
So the mass is conserved. Mass before = mass after.
For example, 40 g of ice that melts makes 40 g of water.
The volume and the density do change, because the particles are arranged differently.

items.meaning: A change where the material recovers its original properties if the change is reversed.
A change that makes new substances. It cannot easily be reversed.

diagram.alt: Sort each change into physical or chemical.
diagram.prompt: Sort each change into physical or chemical.

items.text: Steam condensing on a cold window
Dry ice turning directly into gas

items: Mass is conserved in every change of state, because the particles are only rearranged.
Physical change: the original properties return when the change is reversed.
Chemical change: new substances form and it cannot easily be reversed.

checks.q: What is the name of the change of state from a solid directly to a gas?
100 g of steam condenses. What is the mass of the water formed? Explain your answer.
checks.a: 100 g. Mass is conserved because the particles are only rearranged and the number of particles stays the same.

checks.q: How is a physical change different from a chemical change?
checks.a: In a physical change the material recovers its original properties if the change is reversed. A chemical change cannot easily be reversed.

exam_phrases: particles in a solid are in a regular pattern
particles in a liquid are in a random arrangement
particles in a solid are vibrating about fixed positions
particles in a liquid are moving freely
the potential energy of the particles increases
particles change from being spread apart to touching each other
attractive forces between particles are stronger in a solid than in a liquid

mistakes.wrong: As the ice melts, the particles move further apart, so the density decreases.
mistakes.right: References to density and spacing are ignored. Describe the arrangement (regular to random) and the movement (vibrating about fixed positions to moving freely).

mistakes.wrong: The temperature of the ice rises while it melts.
mistakes.right: The temperature remains constant while it changes to water. The potential energy of the particles increases.

mistakes.wrong: When argon becomes a solid, its particles stop moving.
mistakes.right: Particles in a solid vibrate about fixed positions. They change from moving freely to vibrating.

worked_example.question: Argon in the air changed from a gas to a liquid to a solid as the temperature decreased from 20 °C to –190 °C. Explain the changes in the arrangement and movement of the particles of the argon as the temperature of the air decreased.
answer_points: as the argon cools the particles slow down
gas to liquid: the particles change from being spread apart to touching each other
liquid to solid: the particles change from a random arrangement to a regular pattern
liquid to solid: the particles change from moving freely to vibrating in fixed positions
the (kinetic) energy of the particles decreases with temperature
attractive forces between the particles are stronger in a solid than in a liquid
worked_example.tip: For the top level, explain the changes in arrangement and movement during either cooling or a change of state, and link the points logically.

mistakes.wrong: Evaporation is the change from a solid to a liquid.
mistakes.right: Solid to liquid is melting. Evaporation is liquid to gas. Condensation is gas to liquid. Freezing is liquid to solid.

mistakes.wrong: Sublimation is when a solid changes to a liquid and then to a gas.
mistakes.right: Sublimation is a solid changing directly to a gas or vapour.

mistakes.wrong: Sublimation is the change from a gas to a liquid.
mistakes.right: Gas to liquid is condensation. Sublimation is solid to gas. The reverse, gas to solid, is also accepted.

worked_example.question: Describe what happens when a substance experiences sublimation.
answer_points: a change of state: a solid changes
worked_example.tip: The reverse, gas to solid, is also accepted. An example such as ice to water vapour also scores.

exam_phrases: original properties return if change is reversed

mistakes.wrong: The water has less mass than the ice, because the ice has melted.
mistakes.right: The mass is the same. 40 g of ice makes 40 g of water. Mass is conserved.

mistakes.wrong: Writing only that the mass is conserved, with no reason.
mistakes.right: Add the explanation in terms of particles: they are only rearranged, and the number of particles stays the same.

mistakes.wrong: A physical change can never be reversed.
mistakes.right: A physical change is easily reversible, and the original properties return. It is a chemical change that cannot easily be reversed.

worked_example.question: A student puts an ice cube of mass 40 g into a beaker. The ice cube melts. The mass of the water produced is 40 g. Explain why.
answer_points: mass before = mass after / mass is conserved
the particles are rearranged, and the number of particles stays the same
worked_example.tip: One mark for the idea that mass is conserved and one for the explanation in terms of particles. Atoms or molecules are accepted for particles.
